details.label: Summary
details.text: The threat for at least isolated severe storms capable of severe wind gusts up to 65-80 mph and large hail potentially up to two inches is expected to increase late this afternoon through this evening. A watch is possible

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Visible satellite imagery shows a growing cumulus field from Ogallala north toward Merriman in western NE, in the vicinity of a surface trough. Additional, more elevated convection is noted along the SD-NE border, near Pine Ridge. The 18Z North Platte sounding sampled the presence of an EML with considerable capping for surface-based parcels. Since that observation, surface temperatures have warmed through the 80s into lower 90s, effectively reducing the amount of convective inhibition. Forcing for ascent associated with a subtle short-wave trough currently moving through eastern WY in conjunction with continued daytime heating is expected locally erode the cap such that isolated thunderstorm development will become increasingly likely within the next 1-3 hours along the surface trough and/or cool front moving into the region from the north. The presence of steep low/mid-level lapse rates and a vertically veering wind profile with 30-35 kt of deep-layer shear will support organized storm modes, including supercells with an associated risk for large hail, potentially up to two inches and locally severe wind gusts. Latest time-lagged HRRR and RRFS guidance suggests that a more robust damaging wind threat could materialize this evening as storms merge into clusters, at which point gusts up to 65-80 mph would become more likely

mesoscaleDiscussions.summary: High-based thunderstorms moving off the higher terrain of southeast Wyoming, central Colorado, and far north/northeast New Mexico will pose a risk of severe winds through early evening. Watch issuance is not expected given very limited buoyancy

details.label: Summary
details.text: High-based thunderstorms moving off the higher terrain of southeast Wyoming, central Colorado, and far north/northeast New Mexico will pose a risk of severe winds through early evening. Watch issuance is not expected given very limited buoyancy

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Visible satellite imagery shows steady cumulus development along the CO Front Range within a weak upslope flow regime as well as across southeast WY in proximity to a weak low/mid-level MCV. Recent ACARs soundings from Denver, CO, along with the KFTG VWP, sampled 15-20 knot westerly flow within the CAPE-bearing layer that should promote eastward translation of convection off of the higher terrain through late afternoon. These soundings also sampled very dry boundary-layer conditions with LCLs just under 3 km. Although the very dry low-level conditions are limiting overall buoyancy magnitudes (SBCAPE is generally estimated to be around 250-500 J/kg per mesoanalysis and representative forecast soundings), they are highly favorable for intense downbursts capable of producing swaths of severe winds. This idea is reflected by a collection of recent CAM solutions, which generally depict sporadic swaths of 60-75 mph gusts as convection slowly intensifies and spreads east over the next few hours. The very limited CAPE and modest kinematic environment should modulate convective intensity and longevity (and preclude the need for a watch), and convection should steadily weaken in tandem with nocturnal cooling later this evening

details.label: Summary
details.text: Isolated to widely-scattered thunderstorms are expected to overspread much of the northern Great Basin through early evening. The more intense thunderstorms will be capable of severe downburst winds. However, the overall threat should remain transient/isolated enough to preclude watch issuance

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Over the past hour, GOES imagery has shown a steady uptick in coverage and depth of convective cumulus across the central and northern Great Basin. This comes as temperatures warm into the mid 80s to low 90s and lingering inhibition is eroded. Based on recent surface observations and the recent 18z LKN sounding, MLCAPE values generally between 250-500 J/kg are likely overspreading much of the region, and low-level lapse rates are approaching dry adiabatic with LCLs estimated to be near 2 to 2.5 km. Although buoyancy magnitudes are generally fairly modest, the dry and deeply-mixed boundary layer is favorable for accelerating downdrafts - especially with the deeper convective cores that can be influenced by 30-35 knot mid-level flow above 6 km as sampled by the LKN sounding (which may promote some degree of storm longevity and organization). In general, thunderstorm coverage and longevity is expected to remain fairly limited given weak large-scale forcing for ascent, modest buoyancy, and somewhat weak deep-layer wind shear, but latest CAM ensemble guidance suggests gusts up to 60-75 mph will be possible with the more intense downbursts

details.label: Summary
details.text: Isolated severe storms capable of damaging wind gusts and marginally severe hail appear possible this afternoon into evening. A watch is currently not expected

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Ahead of a vigorous vorticity maximum centered over the Champlain Valley, visible satellite imagery indicates deepening cumulus across the discussion area amidst a warming and destabilizing air mass with around 500 J/kg of MLCAPE. Eventual thunderstorm development is expected later this afternoon as height falls/cooling aloft overspread the warming boundary layer, contributing to further air mass destabilization. The kinematic environment features strong mid/upper-level winds, resulting in long, straight hodographs supportive of splitting supercells with an associated hail risk. Isolated damaging wind gusts also appear possible owing to the steepening low-level lapse rates across the region, which will enhance evaporative cooling in the sub-cloud layer
